chapters.title: Chapter 5: Central Banks in Crisis, and What Investors Learn

lessons.title: The 2022 Global Tightening Cycle: Inflation Returns and Rates Surge

body.text: 2022 was the year cheap money ended everywhere at once. Inflation hit forty-year highs, the Fed raised rates faster than at any time in decades, and the safest assets in the world lost more money than in any year on record. For India it meant a 250 basis point hiking cycle, the worst year for the rupee in Asia, and a stock market that somehow still finished higher.

children.text: The last lesson ended with central banks flooding the world with liquidity. This one is the hangover. It ties together almost everything in this course: inflation targeting from Chapter 1, the toolkit from Chapter 2, the transmission into bonds, stocks and currencies from Chapter 3, and the global central banks from Chapter 4.
Why Inflation Came Back

Three forces arrived together. Pandemic-era stimulus had left households and companies with unusual amounts of cash. Supply chains were still broken, so the supply of goods could not keep up. Then Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, sending energy, food and fertiliser prices sharply higher.

body.text: Central banks initially called the inflation transitory, expecting supply chains to heal. They were wrong, and the delay meant they had to tighten far more aggressively later. That experience is precisely why the RBI and the Fed reacted so quickly to inflation risk in 2026, as you saw in Chapters 1 and 4.

children.text: The Fastest Fed Tightening in Decades

body.title: Add Up the Year
body.prompt: In 2022 the Fed raised rates by 25, 50, 75, 75, 75, 75 and 50 basis points across seven meetings. What was the total tightening, in basis points?
body.explanation: 25 + 50 + 75 + 75 + 75 + 75 + 50 = 425 basis points in a single calendar year, including four consecutive 75 basis point hikes. On top of that, the Fed began quantitative tightening in June 2022, letting up to $95 billion of bonds a month roll off, as you saw in Chapter 4. Rates and the balance sheet were tightening at the same time.

children.text: India Joins the Cycle

The RBI moved later than the Fed but then moved fast. On 4 May 2022, between scheduled meetings, the MPC raised the repo rate by 40 basis points and the CRR by 50 basis points, a double tightening that caught markets by surprise. Hikes continued at every meeting until February 2023.

body.title: Measure the RBI Cycle
body.prompt: The repo rate rose from 4.00% in April 2022 to 6.50% by February 2023. How many basis points of tightening is that?
body.explanation: 6.50% minus 4.00% = 2.50 percentage points = 250 basis points in about ten months. Even so, inflation stayed above 6% for three consecutive quarters, which triggered the RBI failure report to the government that you studied in Chapter 1.

children.text: The RBI was fighting on two fronts. Higher US rates pulled money out of India, so it also sold dollars to slow the rupee. India's forex reserves, which had peaked above $640 billion in September 2021, fell to about $524.5 billion by late October 2022.

body.title: What Did Defending the Rupee Cost?
body.prompt: India's forex reserves fell from about $642 billion at their 2021 peak to about $524.52 billion in late October 2022. What was the percentage fall? Enter a negative number, rounded to one decimal place.
body.explanation: ($524.52 billion − $642 billion) ÷ $642 billion × 100 = about -18.3%. Not all of that was intervention, since a stronger dollar also reduces the reported value of other currencies held in reserves. But it shows why the RBI spent the following years rebuilding reserves, reaching a record $785.71 billion by September 2026.

children.text: When Tightening Broke Something: The UK Gilt Crisis

On 23 September 2022, the new UK government announced a mini-budget with large unfunded tax cuts. Bond investors took fright, and the 30-year gilt yield jumped about 120 basis points in three days, one of the fastest moves ever seen in a major government bond market.

markDefs.definition: A strategy where pension funds use derivatives and borrowing to match long-term obligations, which requires posting more collateral when bond yields rise sharply.

children.text: That exposed a hidden problem. UK pension funds used
liability-driven investment (LDI)

strategies that required them to post more collateral as yields rose. To raise cash they sold gilts, which pushed yields higher still, forcing yet more selling. It was a doom loop, the same self-reinforcing spiral you saw in 2008 and in India in 2018.

body.title: Why Did the Bank of England Buy Bonds While Raising Rates?
body.question: In late September 2022 the Bank of England was raising interest rates to fight inflation, yet it announced emergency purchases of long-dated gilts. Is that contradictory?
options: Yes, it was a policy error that undid its inflation fight
No, the purchases were a targeted financial stability operation to stop a forced-selling spiral, separate from its inflation-fighting rate decisions
No, because buying bonds also fights inflation
Yes, because central banks can only use one tool at a time
body.explanation: Central banks separate monetary policy from financial stability. The gilt purchases were temporary, limited and aimed at preventing a disorderly collapse in the pension system, not at stimulating the economy. The Bank continued raising rates to fight inflation. The episode is a reminder that tightening cycles often break something in a corner of the financial system nobody was watching.

children.text: The Worst Year in Bond Market History

Rising yields mean falling bond prices, and 2022 saw the sharpest, broadest rise in yields in decades. The result was the worst year for global bonds in modern records. Long-dated bonds, with the highest duration, lost the most, exactly as the duration formula from Chapter 3 predicts.

body.text: The traditional 60/40 portfolio, 60% stocks and 40% bonds, is built on the idea that bonds rise when stocks fall. In 2022 both fell together, because the thing hurting stocks, rapidly rising interest rates, was the same thing hurting bonds. Diversification protects against many risks, but not against a global repricing of interest rates.

children.text: Why India Held Up Better
Domestic money replaced foreign money.
Steady SIP inflows from Indian households absorbed much of the record foreign selling.
Banks were in better shape.
After years of cleaning up bad loans, Indian banks entered the cycle with stronger balance sheets, so higher rates did not trigger a credit crunch.
Inflation was high but not extreme.
At its 7.79% peak, India's inflation was far below the 9% to 10% seen in the US and parts of Europe, so the RBI had to tighten less.
Growth held up.
India remained among the fastest growing large economies, which supported corporate earnings even as valuations came under pressure.

body.title: Your 60/40 Portfolio in 2022
body.scenario: It is late 2022. Your portfolio is 60% in an equity index fund and 40% in a long duration debt fund, a mix you chose because bonds were supposed to cushion equity falls. Instead, both have fallen. Your debt fund is down several percent, which you did not think was possible with government bonds, and a colleague says bonds are now broken as a diversifier.
body.prompt: What actually happened, and what would you do now?
body.modelAnswer: Nothing is broken; the diversification simply did not work against this particular shock. Bonds usually cushion equity falls when the problem is weak growth, because central banks then cut rates and bond prices rise. In 2022 the problem was inflation, so central banks raised rates sharply, which hurt both stocks and bonds at once. Your long duration fund fell because of duration: if its modified duration is around 7 and yields rose 2 percentage points, a fall of roughly 14% in price terms is arithmetic, not mismanagement. The question now is forward looking. After the repricing, those same bonds yield far more than before, so future returns are higher and the fund earns that yield while you wait. If you need money soon, or cannot tolerate mark-to-market swings, shifting some money to shorter duration funds reduces sensitivity. If your horizon is long, selling after the fall converts a paper loss into a real one, just as your bonds started offering their best yields in years. The durable lesson is to match duration to your time horizon, rather than expecting bonds to hedge every kind of shock.

body.title: Go Deeper: Why Central Banks Were Late

children.text: Through 2021, both the Fed and the RBI described rising inflation as transitory, driven by temporary supply disruptions and by comparison with the low prices of the pandemic year. On that view, tightening would have been a mistake, since it would have hurt a fragile recovery without fixing supply chains.

Two things went wrong. Supply disruptions lasted far longer than expected, and the war in Ukraine added a fresh energy and food shock in February 2022. By then inflation had spread from goods to services and wages, which monetary policy does affect. The cost of the delay was a much steeper tightening cycle than would have been needed if central banks had started earlier. It is the single biggest reason policymakers in 2026 have been so quick to talk about hikes at the first sign of inflation risk.

body.title: Stress-Test Your Own Portfolio
steps: Find the modified duration of every debt fund you own and estimate the loss if yields rose 2 percentage points
Check what your equity and debt holdings did in calendar 2022, when both fell together
Compare the current repo rate with the 6.50% peak of February 2023 and the 4.00% low of 2020
Note how much of your portfolio depends on interest rates staying low
Write down what you would do if inflation rose above 6% again, before it happens

points: Pandemic stimulus, broken supply chains and the Ukraine war pushed US inflation to a 40-year high of 9.1% in June 2022 and India to 7.79% in April 2022.
The Fed raised rates by 425 basis points across seven meetings in 2022, including four consecutive 75 basis point hikes, while also running quantitative tightening.
The RBI hiked 250 basis points from 4.00% to 6.50% between May 2022 and February 2023, starting with an off-cycle move.
Defending the rupee helped cut India forex reserves from above $640 billion in 2021 to about $524.5 billion by October 2022.
The UK gilt crisis showed how fast tightening can break something unexpected, forcing the Bank of England to buy bonds for stability while still raising rates.
It was the worst year for global bonds in modern records, yet the Nifty still rose about 4.3%, supported by domestic flows even as FPIs sold a record ₹1.21 lakh crore.
